title_en: OPPO Guangdong Mobile Communication Co., Ltd. et al. v. Sharp Corporation et al. — dispute over jurisdiction objection in a standard essential patent licensing dispute
ruling_gist_en: 1. When determining jurisdiction over disputes concerning global licensing conditions for standard essential patents, consideration may be given to: the scope of the parties' intent during licensing negotiations for the standard essential patents involved; the countries of grant and distribution ratios of the standard essential patent rights involved in the licensing negotiations; the principal place of implementation, principal place of business, or principal source of revenue of the implementer of the standard essential patents involved; the place of licensing negotiations; and the location of property subject to attachment or enforcement by the parties, among other factors.

full_text_en:
OPPO Guangdong Mobile Communications Co., Ltd. et al. v. Sharp Corporation et al. — dispute over jurisdiction objection regarding standard essential patent license

Ruling Summary

1. In determining the jurisdiction over a dispute concerning global licensing conditions for standard essential patents, consideration may be given to the scope of the parties’ intent during negotiations on the licensing of the standard essential patents at issue, the countries granting the standard essential patents involved in the licensing negotiations and their distribution proportions, the principal place of implementation, principal place of business, or principal source of revenue of the implementer of the standard essential patents at issue, the place of licensing negotiations, and the location of property of the parties that may be attached or subject to enforcement.

2. Where the parties have the intent to reach a global license and the dispute has a closer connection with China, even if the parties have not reached an agreement on jurisdiction, a Chinese court has the authority, upon application by one party, to make a ruling on the global licensing conditions for standard essential patents.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2020) Supreme People’s Court IP Final Civil Jurisdiction No. 517

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Sharp Corporation. Domicile: 1番地, Takumi-cho, Sakai-ku, Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, Japan.

Representative: Nomura Katsuaki, Executive Vice President and Director of the Corporation.

Agent ad litem: Liu Qinghui, attorney at Beijing Anjie Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wu Li, attorney at Beijing Anjie Law Firm.

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Japan Corporation. Domicile: 19-20, 1-chome, Nishitawabi-cho, Abeno-ku, Osaka City, Osaka Prefecture, Japan.

Representative: Takahara Naoyuki, Head of Legal Department of the Corporation.

Agent ad litem: Chen Zhixing, attorney at Beijing Anjie Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Xu Jing, attorney at King & Wood Mallesons.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): OPPO Guangdong Mobile Communications Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 18, Wusha Haibin Road, Chang’an Town, Dongguan City, Guangdong Province, People’s Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Liu Bo, Manager and Executive Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Ye, attorney at Beijing Jingtian & Gongcheng Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Yu Yuanfang, female, staff member of the Company.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): OPPO Guangdong Mobile Communications Co., Ltd., Shenzhen Branch. Domicile: 7th Floor, Zhuoyue Houhai Financial Center, No. 126 Haide Third Road, Yuehai Street, Nanshan District, Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province, People’s Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Liu Bo, responsible person of the Branch.

Agent ad litem: Huang Yufeng, male, staff member of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Huan, male, staff member of the Company.

Appellants Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation filed an appeal with this Court against the civil ruling (2020) Yue 03 Min Chu No. 689 (hereinafter referred to as the original ruling) rendered by the Shenzhen Intermediate People’s Court of Guangdong Province (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance) on October 16, 2020, in a dispute with Appellees OPPO Guangdong Mobile Communications Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as OPPO Company) and OPPO Guangdong Mobile Communications Co., Ltd., Shenzhen Branch (hereinafter referred to as OPPO Shenzhen Company) over jurisdiction objection regarding standard essential patent license. After the case was docketed on December 7, 2020, this Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and heard the parties on January 14, 2021. The following persons appeared at the hearing: Liu Qinghui and Wu Li, agents ad litem for Sharp Corporation; Chen Zhixing and Xu Jing, agents ad litem for Japan Corporation; Zhao Ye and Yu Yuanfang, agents ad litem for OPPO Company; and Huang Yufeng and Wang Huan, agents ad litem for OPPO Shenzhen Company.

Sharp Corporation’s grounds for appeal: 1. Revoke the original ruling and dismiss the lawsuit filed by OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company; 2. If the above request cannot be fully satisfied, issue a ruling in accordance with the law to dismiss the claims for damages for infringement and the claims for ruling on global licensing conditions for standard essential patents related to WiFi standards, and the claims for ruling on licensing conditions for standard essential patents related to 3G and 4G standards outside the territory of Mainland China; 3. Issue a ruling transferring the dispute over licensing conditions for standard essential patents related to 3G and 4G standards within the territory of Mainland China to the Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court of the People’s Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court) for jurisdiction. Facts and reasons:

First, the place of implementation of the alleged infringement, the place of occurrence of the result, or the domicile of the defendant in the allegations by OPPO Company are all outside Mainland China. Therefore, the lawsuit filed by OPPO Company regarding the infringement dispute does not fall within the jurisdiction of Chinese courts and should be dismissed. This case involves both infringement and standard essential patent licensing. OPPO Company has combined two legal relationships in one claim for court adjudication, which lacks legal basis. As for the standard essential patent licensing dispute, jurisdiction shall be exercised by the court of the defendant’s domicile or the place of performance of the contract. Given that the parties have not yet reached agreement on the key terms of the contract, there is no performance of the contract, and the defendant’s domicile is also outside Mainland China. As for the infringement dispute, jurisdiction shall be exercised by the court of the place of implementation of the infringement, the place of occurrence of the infringement result, or the defendant’s domicile, all of which are abroad. Therefore, OPPO Company has no legal basis for filing the lawsuit in Chinese courts.

Second, this case does not meet the threshold for filing a standard essential patent license dispute. For a standard essential patent license dispute, the threshold should be that the patentee and the patent implementer have conducted full negotiations on the licensing conditions but are still unable to reach an agreement. As of now, the parties are still in the preliminary negotiation stage regarding the licensing of the standard essential patents at issue, far from reaching the level of “full negotiations.”

Third, the court of first instance does not have jurisdiction over this case. 1. Sharp Corporation and OPPO Company have not yet signed a contract, so there is no issue of the place of performance of the contract. The court of first instance’s determination that Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province is the place of implementation of the standard essential patents at issue lacks factual basis. 2. The court of first instance erroneously characterized the dispute over damages for infringement as a dispute over pre-contractual liability, which is factually and legally incorrect. The dispute over pre-contractual liability in this case should be treated similarly to a licensing contract dispute. The subject matter of this action, i.e., the location of Sharp Corporation’s patents, is not in Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province, so the court of first instance has no jurisdiction. Sharp Corporation has no attachable property in Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province, and has no representative office in Mainland China, so the court of first instance also has no jurisdiction over the alleged pre-contractual liability dispute. 3. Even assuming the contrary, OPPO Shenzhen Company is not a party to the licensing negotiations, and the infringement lawsuits filed by Sharp Corporation in Japan, Germany, and the Taiwan region of China do not involve OPPO Shenzhen Company. Even if the indirect result of the alleged infringement occurs in Mainland China, jurisdiction should be determined based on OPPO Company’s domicile, i.e., Dongguan City, Guangdong Province, and the case should be transferred to Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court for trial.

Fourth, even if this dispute meets the conditions for filing, the court of first instance should not rule on the global licensing conditions for standard essential patents related to Sharp Corporation’s WiFi, 3G, and 4G standards. This claim exceeds the jurisdiction of the court of first instance and should be dismissed. Sharp Corporation has filed lawsuits for damages for patent infringement in Japan, Germany, and the Taiwan region of China, and the calculation of damages in those cases may involve royalty rates. These cases were filed earlier than the time when OPPO Company submitted the Supplemental Civil Complaint in this case and are already in the trial process. Under these circumstances, the court of first instance should, on the principle of respect for judicial sovereignty and international comity, decline to address the matter of ruling on global licensing conditions raised by OPPO Company; otherwise, conflicting judgments on royalty rates would result.

Japan Corporation’s appeal: It agrees with and maintains Sharp Corporation’s grounds for appeal, facts, and reasons. It additionally states that the evidence on record cannot establish a disputable jurisdictional nexus between Japan Corporation and this case. Japan Corporation has no relationship with either the infringement dispute or the patent licensing dispute in this case and should not be a defendant. The lawsuit against Japan Corporation by OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company should be dismissed.

OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company jointly responded:

First, the two core claims raised by OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company are, respectively, “to confirm the breach of fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) obligations and to claim damages” and “to determine license fees consistent with FRAND principles.” These two claims represent two sides of the same coin in a standard essential patent licensing dispute. Adjudicating both claims together can thoroughly and completely resolve the licensing dispute at its root.

Second, Chinese courts have jurisdiction over this case. Chinese courts have inherent jurisdiction over the implementation and value of Chinese patents. Chinese courts have the authority to adjudicate the license rates for Chinese patents.

Third, the court of first instance has jurisdiction over this case. 1. A substantial portion of the research and development, sales, offers for sale, and testing activities of OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company occur in Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province. Shenzhen City is one of the principal places of implementation of the standard essential patents at issue. Based on the “place of patent implementation” as a ground for jurisdiction, the court of first instance has jurisdiction over this case in accordance with the law. 2. Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province is the place where the parties’ licensing negotiations took place, which is the place of performance reflecting the characteristics of the contract, and the court of first instance is the convenient court for this case. 3. The act of breaching FRAND obligations is an act that violates the principle of good faith under Chinese law and constitutes a broad form of civil infringement. The acts of Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation in breaching FRAND obligations directly caused OPPO Shenzhen Company, after investing substantial human and material resources, to be unable to smoothly obtain the relevant patent licenses, resulting in economic losses. Therefore, Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province is also the direct place where the infringement results occurred in this case.

Fourth, Chinese courts have the authority to adjudicate the global licensing conditions for the standard essential patents at issue. 1. Standard essential patents are globally distributed, and Chinese courts have factual grounds for adjudicating global licensing conditions. 2. China is the place with the closest connection to this case, and Chinese courts are convenient for jurisdiction. 3. The license offer made by Sharp Corporation to OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company after the initiation of licensing negotiations was also for global licensing conditions, indicating that the parties had formed an intent and consensus for a global license of the standard essential patents at issue. 4. Even assuming the parties did not reach an agreement on jurisdiction, the UK Supreme Court, in its final ruling on August 26, 2020, confirmed that UK courts have jurisdiction over global licensing conditions for relevant standard essential patents. 5. Filing a claim for adjudication of global licensing conditions does not violate any prohibitive legal provisions in China, nor has Chinese law or judicial policy ever explicitly denied Chinese courts’ jurisdiction over global standard essential patent license rates. A ruling on global license rates has a legal basis and is an objective necessity for the one-time resolution of licensing disputes. 6. None of the patent infringement lawsuits filed by Sharp Corporation worldwide include a claim for the court to determine licensing conditions, so the scope of the claims in this case does not directly conflict with other foreign cases.

In summary, OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company request that the appeal be dismissed and the original ruling be upheld.

OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, which accepted and docketed the case on March 25, 2020. OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company requested: 1. To confirm that the relevant acts of Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation in the licensing negotiations constituted a breach of FRAND obligations or the principle of good faith, including but not limited to unreasonable delays in the negotiation process, delays in signing confidentiality agreements, failure to provide claim charts to OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company in accordance with trade practices, concealment of their prior FRAND declarations, unilateral initiation of litigation as a surprise attack without full negotiations, using threats of injunctions in infringement lawsuits to force OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company to accept unilaterally set licensing conditions, and excessively high pricing. OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company reserved the right to pursue other acts by Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation in breach of FRAND obligations or the principle of good faith during the litigation; 2. To adjudicate the licensing conditions for standard essential patents related to WiFi, 3G, and 4G standards owned and authorized by Sharp Corporation for OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company’s smart terminal products on a global scale, including but not limited to the license fee rates; 3. To order Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation to compensate OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company for economic losses totaling RMB 3,000,000 caused by their breach of FRAND obligations.

During the period for submitting the statement of defense, Sharp Corporation raised a jurisdictional objection to the case, requesting: 1. Dismiss the lawsuit; 2. If the above request cannot be fully satisfied, issue a ruling in accordance with the law to dismiss the lawsuit regarding the infringement dispute, transfer the dispute over licensing conditions for Chinese patents within Mainland China to the Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court for jurisdiction, and dismiss the lawsuit regarding licensing conditions for patents in other countries or regions.

Japan Corporation also raised a jurisdictional objection, agreeing with Sharp Corporation’s opinion, and stating that it has no relationship with either the infringement dispute or the patent licensing dispute in this case and should not be a defendant.

The court of first instance, in accordance with Article 18, Article 127, and Article 265 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Civil Procedure Law), ruled: The jurisdictional objections raised by the defendants Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation were rejected. The case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne jointly by the defendants Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation.

Upon preliminary examination, this Court finds the following:

(I) Facts relevant to the jurisdictional dispute in this case

OPPO Shenzhen Company’s business scope includes the development of mobile communication terminal device software and hardware and related supporting services, as well as technical development services for mobile phones and their peripheral products and accessories.

As of December 31, 2019, OPPO Company’s sales in China accounted for 71.08%, sales in Europe accounted for 0.21%, and sales in Japan accounted for 0.07%.

On July 10, 2018, Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation sent a patent list to OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company, comprising a standard essential patent portfolio of 645 3G/4G patent families (555 CN), 13 WiFi patent families (10 CN), and 44 HEVC patent families (45 CN).

On February 19, 2019, OPPO Company, OPPO Shenzhen Company, Sharp Corporation, and Japan Corporation held a meeting at OPPO Shenzhen Company’s office located at 7th Floor, Zhuoyue Houhai Financial Center, No. 126 Haide Third Road, Nanshan District, Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province. A slide presentation used by Sharp Corporation and Japan Corporation during the negotiations indicated that their proposed overall preferred structure for the standard essential patent license was: a term of 5 years, licensed patents (licensed standards) being “3G/4G/Wi-Fi/HEVC standard essential patents owned during the term,” and a license scope of “global non-exclusive license, no sub-licensing rights, limited to the field of implementation using the licensed standards.”

(II) Basic information concerning related foreign lawsuits

After the court of first instance accepted this dispute, OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company filed an application for a preservation order. The court of first instance issued a civil ruling (2020) Yue 03 Min Chu No. 689-1 on October 16, 2020, which found the following facts regarding related lawsuits:

On January 30, 2020, Sharp Corporation filed a patent infringement lawsuit against OPPO Japan Co., Ltd. (OPPO Company’s exclusive agent in Japan) with the Tokyo District Court in Japan, alleging that some OPPO-branded mobile phones sold by OPPO Japan infringed its Japanese Patent No. JP5379269, and requested a judgment prohibiting OPPO Japan from using, transferring, leasing, importing, or exporting, or applying for transfer or leasing of the involved OPPO phones; ordering OPPO Japan to destroy the involved OPPO phones; and bearing the litigation costs. JP5379269 relates to WiFi technology.

On March 6, 2020, Sharp Corporation filed a patent infringement lawsuit against OPPO Japan with the Tokyo District Court, involving Japanese Patent No. JP4659895, and requested a judgment ordering OPPO Japan to pay damages of 300,000,175 yen plus interest and bear the litigation costs. JP4659895 relates to LTE technology.

On March 9, 2020, Sharp Corporation filed an infringement lawsuit in Japan regarding JP4706071, with the same claims as those in the lawsuit filed on March 6, 2020, regarding JP4659895. JP4706071 relates to LTE technology.

On March 6, 2020, Sharp Corporation filed a patent infringement lawsuit in the Munich Court in Germany, alleging that OPPO Company’s production and sales of OPPO Reno2 and other mobile phones constituted patent infringement, and requested a judgment finding OPPO Company infringing, awarding damages for losses since the grant date of its patents, and ordering OPPO Company to bear related litigation costs. The patents involved were EP2854324B1, EP2312896B1, and EP2667676B1, all relating to LTE technology.

On March 6, 2020, Sharp Corporation filed a patent infringement lawsuit against OPPO Company in the Mannheim Regional Court in Germany, involving the same accused products and claims as those in the lawsuit filed on March 6, 2020, in the Munich Court. The patents involved were EP2154903B1 and EP2129181B1, both relating to LTE technology.

On April 1, 2020, Sharp Corporation filed a lawsuit in the Intellectual Property Court of the Taiwan region of China against Samoan Xinmao Global Co., Ltd. (OPPO Company’s exclusive agent in the Taiwan region), requesting a judgment ordering Samoan Xinmao Global to pay damages of NT$2,000,000 plus interest. The patent involved was TWI505663, relating to LTE technology.

On June 28, 2019, Sharp Corporation filed a lawsuit in the Munich Court of Germany against a third party for infringement of its standard essential patents related to LTE, involving patents EP2854324B1, EP2312896B1, and EP2667676B1. During the litigation, Sharp Corporation added requests for injunctions prohibiting the sale, recall, or destruction of infringing products. On September 10, 2020, the Munich Court of Germany issued an injunction against the third party's products based on patent EP2667676B1. Subsequently, Sharp Corporation entered into a standard essential patent license agreement with the third party.

The Court holds that this case is a dispute over jurisdiction for a standard essential patent licensing dispute. Based on the parties' allegations and the preliminary facts found, the issues in dispute during the second instance are: whether Chinese courts have jurisdiction over this case; if Chinese courts have jurisdiction, whether the court of first instance's exercise of jurisdiction is appropriate; if the court of first instance has jurisdiction, whether it is appropriate for it to adjudicate the licensing conditions of the standard essential patents on a global scale in this case; and whether Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. can be a defendant in this case.

(I) Whether Chinese Courts Have Jurisdiction Over This Case

Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. are foreign enterprises with no domicile or representative office within China. For foreign-related civil disputes brought against defendants with no domicile or representative office within China, whether Chinese courts have jurisdiction depends on whether the dispute has an appropriate connection with China. The determination of whether a standard essential patent licensing dispute has an appropriate connection with China should consider the characteristics of such disputes. From judicial practice, such disputes have certain characteristics of contract disputes, such as the need to determine the differences or partial agreements reached by the parties regarding licensing conditions (including royalty rates) based on the negotiation process, and also certain characteristics of patent infringement disputes, such as the need to determine whether the patent subject to licensing is a standard essential patent, whether the standard implementer has implemented such patent, and the validity of such patent. However, the core of a standard essential patent licensing dispute is the request for the court to determine specific licensing conditions or content, with the aim of facilitating the parties to ultimately reach or perform a licensing agreement. Therefore, it can be regarded as a special type of dispute with relatively more contractual characteristics. Considering the above characteristics of such disputes comprehensively, when the defendant is a foreign enterprise with no domicile or representative office within China, the criterion for determining whether the dispute has an appropriate connection with China may consider whether the place of patent grant, place of patent implementation, place of patent license contract execution or negotiation, place of patent license contract performance, or location of seizable or seizable property is within China. As long as one of the above locations is within China, it should be considered that the case has an appropriate connection with China, and Chinese courts have jurisdiction over the case.

In this case, the standard essential patent portfolio subject to licensing involves multiple Chinese patents. The manufacturing activities of OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company implementing the relevant standard essential patents occur in China. The parties once conducted negotiations regarding the licensing of the standard essential patents involved in the case in Shenzhen, China. Therefore, whether as the court of the place of patent grant, the court of the place of implementation of the relevant standard essential patents, or the court of the place of negotiation of the licensing of the relevant standard essential patents, Chinese courts have jurisdiction over this case in accordance with the law. The appeals of Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. arguing that this case is not within the jurisdiction of Chinese courts lack sufficient reasons and are not supported by this Court.

(II) Whether the Court of First Instance's Exercise of Jurisdiction Is Appropriate

As discussed above, a standard essential patent licensing dispute is a special type of dispute with characteristics of both contract disputes and patent infringement disputes. The determination of which Chinese court has jurisdiction over a standard essential patent dispute may consider jurisdictional connections such as the place of patent grant, place of patent implementation, place of patent license contract execution or negotiation, place of patent license contract performance, or location of seizable or seizable property, based on the specific circumstances. In this case, the parties have not yet reached a licensing agreement, so the place of patent license contract execution or performance cannot serve as the jurisdictional connection point. OPPO Shenzhen Company, as a wholly-owned subsidiary of OPPO Company, engages in the development of software and hardware for mobile communication terminal equipment and related supporting services, as well as technical development services for mobile phones and related products and accessories, and is one of the implementing entities of the relevant standard essential patents. OPPO Shenzhen Company is located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, and implements the relevant standard essential patents in that location. Therefore, the court of first instance, as the court of the place of implementation of the relevant standard essential patents, may exercise jurisdiction over this case. At the same time, the parties once conducted negotiations regarding the licensing of the relevant standard essential patents in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, so the court of first instance may also exercise jurisdiction based on being the court of the place of patent license negotiation. The claims of Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. that OPPO Shenzhen Company is not the subject of this dispute, that jurisdiction cannot be determined based on OPPO Shenzhen Company's domicile, and that the licensing dispute over the standard essential patents within mainland China should be transferred to the Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court lack sufficient reasons and are not supported by this Court.

(III) Whether the Court of First Instance Is Appropriate to Adjudicate the Licensing Conditions of the Relevant Standard Essential Patents on a Global Scale in This Case

In this case, OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company filed a lawsuit in the court of first instance, requesting a judgment on the licensing conditions for the standard essential patents related to WiFi standards, 3G standards, and 4G standards owned and authorized to license by Sharp Corporation on a global scale for its smart terminal products, including but not limited to the licensing royalty rate. Upon review, this request complies with the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law regarding conditions for filing a lawsuit and is not a circumstance where the people's court refuses to accept the case as stipulated in the Civil Procedure Law.

Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. appealed, requesting that if their appeal to dismiss OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company's lawsuit cannot be fully granted, the court should rule to dismiss OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company's claims for infringement damages, adjudication of global licensing conditions for WiFi standard-related standard essential patents, and adjudication of licensing conditions for 3G and 4G standard-related standard essential patents outside mainland China. Whether the court of first instance is appropriate to adjudicate the global licensing conditions of the relevant standard essential patents in this case should be comprehensively considered based on the basic facts of the jurisdictional dispute and the special characteristics of standard essential patent licensing disputes. Specifically, the facts found in this case related to the above jurisdictional dispute are as follows:

1. The scope of the parties' intentions during the negotiation of the relevant standard essential patent licensing. During the negotiation process for the licensing of the standard essential patents involved in this case, Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. proposed an overall preferred structure for licensing: a term of 5 years, licensed patents (licensed standards) covering 3G/4G/Wi-Fi/HEVC standard essential patents owned within the term, a global non-exclusive license, no sub-licensing rights, and limited to the field of implementation of the licensed standards. It can be seen that the negotiation content included global licensing conditions for the relevant standard essential patents.

2. The countries granting the standard essential patents involved in the negotiation and their distribution proportions. According to preliminary evidence provided by the parties, this case involves many standard essential patents, most of which are Chinese patents, with some also from the United States, Japan, and other countries.

3. The principal place of implementation, principal place of business, or principal source of revenue of the implementer of the relevant standard essential patents. The principal place of business of OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company is in China, and the manufacturing location and main sales area of their smart terminal products are in China. As of December 31, 2019, OPPO Company's sales in China accounted for 71.08%, sales in Europe accounted for 0.21%, and sales in Japan accounted for 0.07%. From the above data, the sales proportion of OPPO Company's smart terminal products in China is much higher than that in Germany, Japan, and other countries.

4. The place of patent license negotiation or patent license contract execution for the parties. In this case, OPPO Company, OPPO Shenzhen Company, Sharp Corporation, and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. conducted licensing negotiations in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, where OPPO Shenzhen Company is located. Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, can be considered the place of patent license negotiation for the parties.

5. The location of seizable or seizable property of the parties. OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company, as the requesting party for the patent license, have seizable or seizable property within China.

Based on the above facts, first, the parties in this case have the intention to reach global licensing conditions for the relevant standard essential patents and have conducted licensing negotiations on this. The scope of the parties' negotiation intentions constitutes the factual basis for determining the global licensing conditions of the relevant standard essential patents in this case. Second, the standard essential patent licensing dispute in this case obviously has a closer connection with China. Specifically, in this case, most of the standard essential patents involved in the parties' licensing negotiations are Chinese patents; China is the principal place of implementation, principal place of business, or principal source of revenue of the implementer of the relevant standard essential patents; China is the place of patent license negotiation for the parties; and China is also the location of seizable or seizable property of the requesting party for the patent license. Adjudication by a Chinese court of the global licensing conditions of the relevant standard essential patents is not only more conducive to finding the facts regarding OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company's implementation of the relevant standard essential patents but also facilitates the execution of the judgment. Finally, it should also be noted that if the parties can reach an agreement on the adjudication of global licensing conditions for standard essential patents by a court of a particular country, that court can certainly have jurisdiction and adjudicate the global licensing conditions for standard essential patents between the parties. However, a jurisdictional agreement is not a necessary condition for a specific court to have jurisdiction and handle global licensing conditions for standard essential patents. When the parties have the intention to reach a global license and the case has a closer connection with the Chinese court, the court of first instance, based on its jurisdiction over this case, determining that it is appropriate to adjudicate the global licensing conditions of the relevant standard essential patents is not improper. Therefore, the appeal ground of Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. that the royalty rate should be adjudicated separately lacks sufficient reasons and is not supported by this Court.

Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. also appealed, arguing that Sharp Corporation had already filed patent infringement damages lawsuits against OPPO Company in Japan, Germany, and the Taiwan region of China, and that calculating the amount of damages may involve the issue of royalty rates, so the acceptance of this case would conflict with the prior lawsuits. The Court holds that, first, based on the facts found, the patents involved in the above lawsuits are all patents in the jurisdictions where the alleged patent infringement occurred, and the core issue of those disputes is whether patent infringement is constituted, which are typical patent infringement lawsuits. In contrast, the standard essential patent portfolio in this case involves Chinese, US, Japanese, and other patents, and the essence of the dispute is primarily the determination of global licensing conditions for the relevant standard essential patents. The core issues in dispute between this case and the above extraterritorial lawsuits are clearly different. If an extraterritorial court finds infringement in a related patent infringement lawsuit, it can generally only render a judgment on damages for the infringement that has already occurred, whereas this case requires determining patent licensing conditions, which is significantly different in nature from infringement damages. Second, Article 533(1) of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "For a case over which both a Chinese court and a foreign court have jurisdiction, if one party sues in the foreign court and the other party sues in the Chinese court, the people's court may accept the case. After judgment is rendered, if the foreign court applies or a party requests the people's court to recognize and enforce the judgment or ruling of the foreign court on the case, the request shall not be granted, unless otherwise provided by an international treaty to which both parties are signatories or parties." According to the above provision, even if parallel proceedings of a certain case are being heard in a foreign court, as long as the Chinese court has jurisdiction over the case in accordance with the law, the parallel proceedings in the foreign court do not, in principle, affect the Chinese court's exercise of jurisdiction over the case. Therefore, this appeal ground of Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. also lacks factual and legal basis and is not supported by this Court.

(IV) Whether Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. Can Be a Defendant in This Case

According to Article 119 of the Civil Procedure Law, as long as the plaintiff can provide a clear defendant and satisfies other conditions for acceptance, the people's court shall accept the case. In this case, OPPO Company and OPPO Shenzhen Company claim that the acts of Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. and Sharp Corporation in violation of FRAND obligations during the negotiation process directly caused economic losses to OPPO Shenzhen Company, constituting infringement. Based on the preliminary facts found, Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. participated together with Sharp Corporation in the negotiation process for the licensing of the relevant standard essential patents, which is sufficient to establish an arguable jurisdictional connection point between Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. and this case. The court of first instance's ruling that Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. can be a defendant in this case is not improper. As for Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd.'s claim that it is not the patentee and has no connection with this dispute, this can be determined during the substantive hearing of this case.

In summary, the appeals of Sharp Corporation and Saienbeiji Japan Co., Ltd. are not sustainable and should be dismissed; the ruling of the court of first instance has clear factual findings and correct application of law, and should be upheld. Pursuant to Article 170(1)(i) and Article 171 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

Appeal dismissed; original ruling upheld.

This ruling is final.
